paper.title: When Vision Meets Graphs: A Survey on Graph Reasoning and Learning
paper.summary: Graphs are a fundamental data structure underlying many problems in the natural and social sciences. Over the past decade, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have dominated graph machine learning, supported by solid theoretical foundations. Yet scientists often understand graph structure through vision: chemists read molecular diagrams and social scientists inspect network visualizations. Despite decades of work on graph visualization, most graph learning pipelines still treat graphs purely as symbolic structures, rarely leveraging the visual form of graphs. We argue that this gap deserves renewed attention in the era of powerful vision and vision-language models. This survey provides a first systematic overview of the emerging area we term vision meets graphs, which treats visual depictions of graphs as first-class inputs for reasoning and learning. We organize existing work into three threads. Vision for Graph Reasoning studies how models can use visual depictions of graphs to understand structure and carry out multi-step reasoning. Vision for Graph Learning explores how visual features can complement or augment graph encoders beyond known limitations of message passing. Scientific Graphs examines domains where standardized depiction conventions support both reasoning and learning. Our goal is to clarify what current methods can and cannot do, and to outline a path toward foundation models that perceive and reason about graphs as scientists do.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the lack of systematic integration of visual graph representations into machine learning pipelines, which currently treat graphs as purely symbolic structures despite the human tendency to interpret them visually.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Limitations of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in capturing global structural information and the underutilization of visual modality for graph reasoning in the era of Vision-Language Models (VLMs).
analysis.executive_summary: This survey identifies a critical gap in graph machine learning where visual depictions are ignored, despite being a primary mode of human understanding. It proposes a new framework, 'vision meets graphs,' that leverages powerful vision models to enhance graph reasoning and learning beyond the constraints of standard message passing mechanisms.

technical_breakdown.method: Systematic categorization of existing literature into three threads: Vision for Graph Reasoning, Vision for Graph Learning, and Scientific Graphs, focusing on using visual depictions as first-class inputs.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Conceptual framework organizing work around the intersection of vision models (VLMs) and graph structures, rather than a specific neural network architecture.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Review of methods that use visual features to complement graph encoders, multi-step reasoning via visual structure understanding, and domain-specific standardized depiction conventions.

paper.title: FlowTT: Exploiting Computation Flow Reuse in Irregular Tensor-Train Embedding
paper.summary: Tensor-Train (TT) decomposition effectively compresses large embedding tables in recommendation models, but TT-based embedding lookup remains inefficient because partially shared computation flows across input indices are not fully reused and intermediate results are repeatedly materialized off-chip between sequential TT-core contractions. We present FlowTT, a flow-aware GPU execution framework that reformulates TT gather as a set of prefix-shared irregular computation flows. FlowTT combines flow-aligned prefix-based index grouping, a fused TT-embedding execution path with on-chip intermediate retention, and persistent-thread scheduling with chunk-based work stealing and L2 checkpointing to preserve reuse under skewed workloads. By co-designing task formation, data buffering, and scheduling with the structure of TT gather, FlowTT reduces redundant TT-core operations, global-memory traffic, and load imbalance. On Meta's synthetic recommendation benchmarks (Meta-240, Meta-480, and Meta-788), FlowTT consistently achieves the lowest latency compared to existing methods. At batch size 32,768, it reduces latency by up to 42.2% in inference and 49.2% in training relative to EcoRec, while also achieving the lowest inference peak memory usage. These results show that exposing prefix-shared computation is key to efficient TT-based embedding execution.
paper.comment: 9 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables. Accepted to IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD 2026)

analysis.problem_statement: TT-based embedding lookup is inefficient due to the failure to reuse partially shared computation flows across input indices and the repeated off-chip materialization of intermediate results during sequential TT-core contractions.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Memory bandwidth and compute redundancy in large-scale embedding table lookups for recommendation systems.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the inefficiency of Tensor-Train (TT) decompositions in recommendation systems by exploiting prefix-shared computation flows. It is significant for the AI landscape as it optimizes the execution of compressed embeddings on GPUs, reducing latency and memory usage for large-scale recommendation models.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Latency reduction in inference and training

technical_breakdown.method: FlowTT reformulates TT gather as prefix-shared irregular computation flows, combining flow-aligned index grouping, fused execution with on-chip intermediate retention, and persistent-thread scheduling.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Flow-aware GPU execution framework with fused TT-embedding path, on-chip intermediate retention, and L2 checkpointing.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Flow-aligned prefix-based index grouping, chunk-based work stealing, and persistent-thread scheduling to preserve reuse under skewed workloads.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Reduces redundant TT-core operations and global-memory traffic; specific computational complexity not explicitly stated but implies reduced memory access overhead.

paper.title: MakoXC: Rearchitecting DFT Exchange-Correlation with Matrix-Aligned and Knowledge-Organized Sparsity
paper.summary: Density Functional Theory (DFT) is indispensable for materials science and drug discovery, yet the exchange--correlation (XC) evaluation remains a major bottleneck due to its cubic scaling. Although linear-scaling methods exploit electronic nearsightedness to reduce asymptotic complexity, they produce irregular sparse workloads that hide implicit sparsity and prevent efficient use of modern AI accelerators. We present MakoXC, a modular matrix-aligned XC evaluation engine that rearchitects nearsightedness-induced sparsity into regular, accelerator-friendly computations. MakoXC co-designs three key techniques: (1) Matrix-Aligned Cells reorganize nearsightedness-induced interactions into dense, accelerator-aligned data clusters; (2) Sparsity-Guided Activation translates deeper implicit sparsity into numerically correct structured execution for practical linear scaling; and (3) Kernel-Fused Pipeline consolidates fragmented workloads into a unified, compute-intensive execution path that fully unleashes accelerator throughput. Extensive evaluations show that MakoXC achieves average speedups of 67.8$\times$ speedup over standard XC evaluation and 4.7$\times$ over state-of-the-art linear-scaling methods. When integrated into a production-grade commercial DFT package, MakoXC scales XC evaluation to ubiquitin (1,231 atoms, def2-SVP) on 64 GPUs, enabling the end-to-end DFT calculation to complete in under five minutes. By restructuring XC evaluation into a unified, structured computation, MakoXC demonstrates how scientific workloads can achieve genuine low complexity while maximizing parallel efficiency on AI accelerators.
paper.comment: Accepted in the International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage, and Analysis (SC'26)

analysis.problem_statement: Standard linear-scaling Density Functional Theory (DFT) methods generate irregular sparse workloads that fail to efficiently utilize modern AI accelerators due to hidden implicit sparsity.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Memory bandwidth and compute utilization inefficiencies caused by irregular sparse matrix operations on GPU/accelerator hardware.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap between theoretical linear-scaling algorithms and practical hardware efficiency in scientific computing. By restructuring irregular sparse data into dense, accelerator-aligned clusters, it enables high-throughput execution of DFT calculations on AI accelerators, significantly reducing the time for large-scale molecular simulations.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Speedup over standard and linear-scaling baselines
key_metrics.baseline: Standard XC evaluation and state-of-the-art linear-scaling methods

technical_breakdown.method: MakoXC rearchitects exchange-correlation (XC) evaluation by co-designing data layout and execution strategies to transform irregular sparsity into regular, dense computations suitable for GPUs.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Modular matrix-aligned XC evaluation engine featuring Matrix-Aligned Cells, Sparsity-Guided Activation, and a Kernel-Fused Pipeline.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses Matrix-Aligned Cells to cluster interactions into dense blocks; Sparsity-Guided Activation ensures numerical correctness for linear scaling; Kernel-Fused Pipeline consolidates fragmented workloads into unified compute-intensive paths.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Achieves practical linear scaling for XC evaluation, enabling end-to-end DFT calculations for 1,231 atoms on 64 GPUs in under five minutes.
